In the explorer, every measure can be shown after transitions or oddballs, grouped by instructions or by a median split of any of the five questionnaires (within each instruction condition or across all participants), for all trials or the first and second half of the session, with two measures side by side. A second view shows the net placements of a single participant trial by trial.

A transition is the first trial of a new episode (not the first episode of the session); an oddball is a trial with a displaced attack within an episode. The window runs from two trials before to four trials after the event trial (0). After the event, it ends at the next event; before it, trials that are events themselves are left out. 688 transitions and 1,356 oddballs of 86 participants.

Questionnaire effects by lag, within and between conditions

children.label: Questionnaire effects by lag, within and between conditions

children.value: The median-split figures above suggest that the questionnaire scores relate to the course of the error, the replayed state uncertainty and the placement duration differently in the three instruction conditions. These patterns are tested here with models (

For each measure, event type, score and lag (or window), a participant-level regression of the participant mean on the score (z) × condition (contrasts C3 vs C1+C2 and C2 vs C1), with HC3 standard errors. From it: the slope per SD within None, Partial and Full, and the three pairwise differences of the slopes; across conditions, the slope of the model with condition as a covariate. The windows are before the event (k = −2, −1), the event trial (k = 0), the first trial after it (t+1), the mean of t+2 to t+4 (
(late minus t+1). Scores: the general factor (one test per measure) and, alongside, the five questionnaires.

children.alt: Distance from the target: slope per SD of the score within each condition, at each trial relative to the event (95 % CI; ring: p < .05, uncorrected). Top: transitions; bottom: oddballs.

children.value: Distance from the target: slope per SD of the score within each condition, at each trial relative to the event (95 % CI; ring: p < .05, uncorrected). Top: transitions; bottom: oddballs.
Distance from the target after transitions: a condition-specific pattern in Partial.
With the rules mentioned (Partial), higher scores go with a larger distance on the event trial and at t+1 and a smaller distance at t+2:
event trial (k = 0), whose placement was made before the transition was seen, so a larger distance means a placement closer to the old state: general factor +9.3° per SD (p = .006);
t+1: general factor +8.3° (p = .043), OCI +8.0° (p = .005), STICSA state +8.1° (p = .002);
the late window: STICSA trait −5.3° (p = .024), general factor −4.5° (p = .055).

The drop from t+1 to the late window is therefore larger with higher scores (recovery: STICSA trait −12.7° per SD, p = .008; STICSA state −12.1°, p < .001; OCI −11.6°, p = .003; general factor −12.9°, p = .014). In the profile the slope is largest at t+2 (STICSA trait −8.6° per SD, p = .009). At t+3 and t+4 it points the same way but is smaller and not significant (−4.0° and −3.5°, p ≥ .20). With the median split of STICSA trait in Partial, high scorers are closer to the target at t+2 (−17.3°, p = .024) and t+3 (−13.9°, p = .037), and at t+4 the difference is −7.0° (p = .43). They are also closer before the event (k = −1: −16.7°, p = .022). In None the slopes are close to zero at every lag. In Full the late distance is larger with higher scores (OCI +7.7°, p = .047), so the late slope and the recovery differ between Partial and Full (general factor, late: p = .012; recovery: p = .041; OCI, recovery: p = .008).

After oddballs in Partial the distance is smaller with higher STICSA trait before the event (k = −2: p = .037) and on the event trial (p = .028), so part of the Partial pattern is a general difference in accuracy rather than a response to the event.

Replayed state uncertainty: a difference in level, not in the course.

In Partial the uncertainty tends to be lower with higher scores, and in Full higher, already before the event (STICSA trait, before transitions: Partial −0.039 per SD, p = .10; Full +0.025, p = .23; difference p = .042; before oddballs: difference p = .035; OCI similar). The decrease after the event does not differ with the scores in Partial (recovery p ≥ .25). In Full, the uncertainty after transitions decreases less with higher OCI (recovery +0.12, p = .014). The replayed uncertainty is computed from each participant’s fitted parameters, so a difference in level reflects a participant-level property of the model (how the participant’s parameters weigh evidence) rather than the trial-by-trial response.

Across participants within each condition, the late distance and the late uncertainty are correlated after transitions (Spearman ρ = .57, .37 and .48 in None, Partial and Full) and after oddballs in None (ρ = .65). With the late uncertainty as a covariate, the STICSA trait slope of the late distance in Partial changes little (−5.3° to −4.4° per SD), so the uncertainty level does not account for the faster recovery.

children.value: Placement duration: slope per SD of the score within each condition by lag, as in
Placement duration: longer in Full, mostly a general level.

With full instructions, higher scores go with longer placements after transitions (general factor at t+1 +0.32 s per SD, p = .009; late +0.27 s, p = .005; differs from Partial, p = .049 and .038). The slope is of a similar size before the event (+0.23 s, p = .062) and after oddballs (t0 +0.19 s, p = .029; t+1 +0.22 s, p = .045), and the recovery does not change with the scores (p = .43). Higher-scoring participants with full instructions are thus slower throughout, slightly more so after transitions. In None and Partial the slopes are not significant (OCI in Partial on the oddball trial: −0.29 s, p = .016).
General factor and STICSA trait: transitions and stable trials

children.label: General factor and STICSA trait: transitions and stable trials

children.value: The same analysis for the general factor and for STICSA trait: median splits around transitions, and the score slopes within each condition on participant means over
(not an event and at least five trials after the last one) and over the event windows (t0 to t+4 pooled).
Stable trials: closer to the target with higher scores in Partial.

Within the event windows the distance slopes are small in all conditions (Partial: general factor −0.8°, p = .62; STICSA trait −2.1°, p = .19). The placement duration is longer with higher scores in Full on stable trials (general factor +0.22 s, p = .057; STICSA trait +0.21 s, p = .11) and in the event windows (general factor +0.24 s, p = .032).
General factor: high scorers are further from the new state on the event trial (+16.6°, p = .015) and at t+1 (+18.2°, p = .029), closer at t+2 (−10.1°, p = .20), and equal at t+3 and t+4.

STICSA trait: high scorers are closer to the target before the transition (k = −1: −16.7°, p = .022), further on the event trial (+14.2°, p = .019), equal at t+1 (+4.6°, p = .58), and closer at t+2 (−17.3°, p = .024) and t+3 (−13.9°, p = .037).
Replayed uncertainty is lower for high STICSA-trait scorers in Partial at every lag except t+1 (−0.05 to −0.11) and higher in Full (+0.08 to +0.25), with p between .09 and .52 for the single lags.

The smaller distance on stable trials with higher scores in Partial is already there in episodes 1 to 4 (general factor −6.2° per SD, p = .002; STICSA trait −7.4°, p < .001; Full vs Partial p = .011 and .003) and of similar size in episodes 6 to 9 (general factor −6.1°, p = .20; STICSA trait −8.0°, p = .064). With the rules mentioned, higher scores go with a lower precision weighting (Nexus: general factor −0.145 per SD, p = .023; lam: −0.167, p = .009) and a lower expected switch rate h_switch (Nexus: general factor −0.026, p = .042; Full vs Partial p = .019; STICSA trait −0.027, p = .025). With full instructions, noise reactivity of the lam variant is higher with the general factor (+0.233, p = .022). Within Partial, the score effect on the stable-trial distance is not carried by precision weighting: a higher precision weighting goes with a smaller distance (−13.3° per SD of the parameter, p = .003), so with it in the model the score effect becomes larger (general factor −5.8° to −8.5°). With the cue sensitivity (Nexus: −5.8° to −4.0°) or the placement noise of lam (−5.8° to −3.4°) in the model it becomes smaller; the score is not associated with these parameters (p ≥ .15).
Transfer to the other colour cue.

On the first trial with the other cue after a transition, the distance from the new target is larger with higher scores across conditions (general factor +7.1° per SD, p = .014; STICSA trait +7.1°, p = .006), in None (STICSA trait +7.2°, p = .031) and Full (+11.3°, p = .016) more than in Partial (+3.4°, p = .48). On the first trial with the cue of the transition the scores make no difference (p ≥ .39).

On stable trials with the rules mentioned, gaze is more confined to the task locations with higher scores: less gaze beyond the task locations in the prediction window (general factor −0.043, p = .004; Full vs Partial p = .017), less at the third location (−0.009, p = .017; Full vs Partial p = .011) and a lower gaze entropy in the anticipation window (−0.097 bits, p = .048). In Full these slopes are positive and not significant. The spread of the nets (circular variance) differs between Partial and Full with STICSA trait (p = .047; Partial −0.030, Full +0.029), and the number of nets with both scores (Full vs Partial p = .051 and .041). The cursor measures do not change with the scores in Partial or Full; in None, the first movement is more curved with STICSA trait (+0.12, p = .045) and the time after the first net is longer (+0.24 s, p = .026). The longer placements in Full are not clearly located in the time to the first net (+0.07 s, p = .35) or the time after it (+0.08 s, p = .37).

The fit advantage of the Nexus model over simple tracking does not change with the scores in any condition (p ≥ .14). Rule noticed and instructions clear do not change with the scores (p ≥ .16). The aversiveness rises less from the first to the second half with higher general factor in Full (−17.8 points per SD, p = .001) and more in None (+10.2, p = .037; Full vs Partial p = .049).

With the rules mentioned (Partial), higher scores go with a more accurate placement in stable phases and a lower replayed state uncertainty, with placements that stay at the old state on the event trial and t+1 and are back at or below the low scorers’ distance from t+2. With full instructions the direction reverses: higher uncertainty, a tendency to larger distances late after transitions, and longer placements throughout. Without rules the scores make little difference. This fits a stronger reliance on an internal representation of the structure that helps when the structure has to be inferred (Partial) but not when it is given explicitly (Full).
